title: Episode 15: The Texas Archives War: How Mrs. Eberly Fired a Six-Pound Cannon in Austin
description:
In December 1842, Texas President Sam Houston sent a secret military detachment to sneak the national archives out of Austin at midnight. Boarding house owner Angelina Eberly spotted the wagons, ran to Congress Avenue, and fired a loaded six-pound town defense cannon directly into the Land Office, mobilizing the citizens to preserve Austin as the permanent capital of Texas.

FULL TRANSCRIPT:

[Rebecca - Host]
Welcome to Most Fascinating Stories. I'm Rebecca. Every American state has colorful legends surrounding its capital, but only Texas can claim that its permanent seat of government was saved by a pistol-packing, cannon-firing boarding house owner. In eighteen forty-two, the Republic of Texas was locked in a bitter political tug-of-war between President Sam Houston and the citizens of Austin. Houston hated the frontier outpost of Austin, viewing it as dangerously vulnerable to Mexican cavalry raids and Comanche war parties. Determined to move the capital back to his namesake city, Houston sent a secret military expedition to sneak the national archives out of town under cover of darkness. He did not count on Mrs. Angelina Eberly, a six-foot-tall boarding house keeper who ran into the center of Congress Avenue, lit a match, and fired an eight-hundred-pound artillery cannon directly into the Land Office to sound the alarm. Here is George with the story.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT I: A CAPITAL ON THE FRONTIER
In eighteen thirty-nine, the second President of the Republic of Texas, Mirabeau B. Lamar, envisioned a grand empire stretching all the way to the Pacific Ocean. To stake that claim, Lamar moved the national capital from the swampy Gulf Coast city of Houston to a remote, scenic settlement on the Colorado River called Waterloo, renaming it Austin. Lamar's critics were utterly horrified by the decision. Austin was situated squarely on the dangerous western frontier of Texas, exposed to violent raids by powerful Comanche war bands to the north and west, and sitting within striking distance of Mexican cavalry forces across the Rio Grande. Government clerks worked with loaded pistols on their desks, and legislators occasionally had to dodge arrows while walking between government buildings. In eighteen forty-one, General Sam Houston was re-elected President of Texas on a platform of fiscal conservatism and border defense. Houston despised the frontier capital. He openly called Austin 'the most unfortunate site on Earth for a government,' warning that an enemy army could easily sweep in, burn the archives, and capture the entire government in an afternoon. Houston was determined to move the government, its officials, and its sacred national archives back to the safety of the coastal plains. Waterloo had been a tiny settlement of four log cabins when Lamar purchased the land, transforming it into a planned city named in honor of the Father of Texas, Stephen F. Austin. Despite the extreme danger of Comanche attacks, Lamar had personally selected the site while hunting buffalo along the Colorado River, convinced that Texas must project sovereign power westward.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT II: THE MEXICAN RAIDS OF 1842
Sam Houston's dire warnings seemed prophetic in the spring of eighteen forty-two. In March, a Mexican cavalry force of five hundred men under General Rafael Vásquez swept across the Rio Grande, capturing San Antonio without resistance before retreating. Six months later, in September, an even larger Mexican army of fifteen hundred soldiers under French-born General Adrián Woll stormed San Antonio again, capturing sixty prominent Texas district judges, attorneys, and legislators. Austin was thrown into blind panic. Citizens hastily evacuated women and children, while rumors spread that Woll's cavalry was marching directly upon the capital. Taking advantage of the crisis, President Houston refused to convene the Texas Congress in Austin, summoning lawmakers instead to the eastern town of Washington-on-the-Brazos. Houston officially declared Austin an active war zone and ordered the national archives—consisting of sacred constitutional treaties, land grants, army records, and diplomatic correspondence—to be evacuated immediately. The citizens of Austin, however, smelled a political trap. They knew that without the national archives, Austin would lose its legal status as the national capital, turning their frontier town into an abandoned ghost city overnight. The Austin city council formed a Committee of Vigilance, vowing that the archives would leave Austin only over their dead bodies. Houston openly mocked the citizens of Austin in his public speeches, stating that a government could not function from a frontier camp where howling wolves competed with legislative debates. The Mexican army's lightning raids proved that the frontier was still contested ground, sparking fiery debates across Texas regarding the permanence of the new capital.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT III: THE VIGILANCE COMMITTEE AND THE CANNON
The citizens of Austin took extraordinary measures to protect the papers. They placed armed sentries outside the General Land Office day and night, boarding up windows and locking all records in heavy iron vaults. To defend against potential attacks, the town had previously hauled a six-pound iron field artillery cannon onto the intersection of Congress Avenue and Pecan Street—now known as Sixth Street. The cannon was kept permanently loaded with powder and canister shot, positioned to defend the center of town. Prominent among Austin's defenders was Mrs. Angelina Eberly. Mrs. Eberly was a formidable, highly respected widow who operated the Eberly House, the premier hotel and boarding house in Austin. Standing nearly six feet tall, fiercely intelligent, and fiercely loyal to Austin, Mrs. Eberly counted senators, cabinet ministers, and Supreme Court justices among her boarders. She had invested her life savings into property in Austin and was determined that Sam Houston's political scheming would not destroy the community she loved. For months, an uneasy standoff persisted: Houston repeatedly demanded the archives, and Austin's armed vigilance committee repeatedly refused to release them. Mrs. Eberly had arrived in Texas during the early colonial settlement under Stephen F. Austin, surviving frontier hardships, Indian raids, and the Texas Revolution with unshakeable courage.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT IV: THE MIDNIGHT HEIST
Frustrated by the stubborn defiance of the townspeople, President Houston decided to bypass legal channels and take the archives by stealth. In December of eighteen forty-two, Houston secretly commissioned two trusted military officers, Captain Thomas Smith and Captain Eli Chandler. He gave them command of a heavily armed twenty-man cavalry detachment with three heavy freight wagons, issuing sealed military orders: They were to ride into Austin under cover of darkness, load the national archives into the wagons as quickly and quietly as possible, and escape eastward toward Washington-on-the-Brazos before the townspeople woke up. On the freezing, moonless night of December thirtieth, eighteen forty-two, Captain Smith's wagons slipped quietly into Austin. The soldiers used muffled lanterns and skeleton keys to unlock the General Land Office on Congress Avenue. Moving with stealth, they began hauling heavy wooden crates and leather-bound ledgers out the back door, loading them into the wagons. It was nearly two o'clock in the morning. The town was asleep, and it appeared that Houston's secret raid was going to succeed without a hitch. The soldiers had muffled their horses' hooves with gunny sacks and coated wagon axles with axle grease to prevent any sound from alerting the sleeping residents of Congress Avenue.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT V: THE SHOT THAT SAVED AUSTIN
Unfortunately for Sam Houston, Mrs. Angelina Eberly was a light sleeper. Awakened by the clinking of harness chains and the muffled whispering of men outside the Land Office, Mrs. Eberly looked out the second-story window of her boarding house. To her outrage, she spotted armed soldiers loading the national records into three large freight wagons. Mrs. Eberly did not waste time screaming or running to wake the town marshal. Instead, she threw a heavy wool shawl over her nightgown, grabbed a burning torch and a match from her fireplace, and sprinted down Congress Avenue into the cold night air. She ran straight to the loaded six-pound town defense cannon sitting in the middle of the street. Aiming the artillery barrel directly down Congress Avenue toward the front steps of the Land Office, Mrs. Eberly applied the burning match to the touchhole. The cannon detonated with a deafening, thunderous roar that shattered windows for blocks and shook the entire town of Austin out of its beds. A hail of canister shot tore into the brick facade of the Land Office, gouging chunks of stone from the walls and peppering the sides of the wagons. Captain Smith and his terrified soldiers leapt into their saddles, cracked their whips, and fled the city at full gallop with whatever crates were already loaded. The six-pounder iron cannon, originally cast in New Orleans, sent a violent blast of grape and canister whistling down Congress Avenue, terrifying the soldiers and shattering glass across the capital.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VI: THE CHASE TO KINNEY'S FORT AND PEACE
The cannon blast accomplished precisely what Mrs. Eberly intended: within five minutes, every able-bodied man in Austin was in the street with loaded rifles and shotguns. Led by local sheriff Mark Lewis, an armed posse of thirty angry frontiersmen mounted their fastest horses, hauling a small field howitzer behind them in furious pursuit. Captain Smith's freight wagons were bogged down by heavy mud along the Brushy Creek trail. Eighteen miles north of Austin, near Kinney's Fort in modern-day Round Rock, the Austin posse overtook the military detachment and surrounded them. Outnumbered and staring into the barrel of an artillery piece, Captain Smith surrendered without firing a shot. The Austin posse loaded the precious archives back into the wagons, brought them triumphantly back to Austin, and locked them securely inside Mrs. Eberly's hotel cellar. Sam Houston admitted defeat, realizing that attempting to take the archives by force would ignite a localized civil war within Texas. In eighteen forty-five, Texas was annexed by the United States, and in eighteen fifty, a statewide referendum officially confirmed Austin as the permanent capital of Texas. Today, a magnificent bronze statue of Mrs. Angelina Eberly stands proudly on Congress Avenue in downtown Austin, depicting the brave widow with her match held high, forever honoring the woman who fired a cannon to keep Austin on the map. The bronze statue of Angelina Eberly in downtown Austin serves as an immortal symbol of the fierce local pride and frontier independence that defines the spirit of Texas.

[Rebecca - Host]
CONCLUSION
The Texas Archives War is a delightfully defiant chapter of American history that proves you should never underestimate a determined frontier woman with an artillery piece. Thanks to Mrs. Eberly's aim, Austin remained the capital of the Lone Star State. Thank you for listening to Most Fascinating Stories. I'm Rebecca. Join us next time for another forgotten chapter of history. Until then, stay curious.
